passage:
Counsellor's note, Thursday.
Imran, second year, came in about choosing between two electives, Japanese and Urban Photography. Registration closes Monday. He brought a folder of printouts: forum threads, seniors' reviews, a spreadsheet with eleven columns. He said he had read over two hundred comments. "One says the Japanese exam is brutal, the next says it's easy. One senior says photography changed their life, another says it's a waste." He talked fast and kept rubbing his forehead. "What if I pick wrong and regret it for the whole degree?" His friend Chetan had chosen in ten minutes, and that seemed to bother him even more.
What I did next: I put the folder aside and asked him to write, without looking at anything, why he had wanted each elective in the first place. He wrote "I love taking photos" before anything else. I asked him to register by Friday and to come back if it went badly.

qa.q: How many comments did Imran say he had read?
qa.a: Over two hundred comments.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling as he talked about the electives?
qa.a: He was confused and anxious, afraid of regretting a wrong choice for the whole degree; he talked fast and kept rubbing his forehead.

qa.q: Why did putting the folder aside help?
qa.a: It stopped the flood of conflicting opinions and brought back Imran's own first reason, "I love taking photos", which was clearer than any review.

qa.q: What would change if Imran kept reading forums until Monday?
qa.a: He would probably find even more contradicting comments, feel more doubt and dread, and still face the same choice at the deadline.

grounding: Shows a young adult who reads endless reviews before choosing an elective and ends up more confused and afraid of regret.

subtype: Naming the unknowns and a default [Response]
passage: I'm Gopika, and I share a hostel room with Preeti, so I watched her whole method on Tuesday. She had two offers for the summer: the marine lab in Goa or the river-cleaning NGO back home in Patna. Instead of pacing, she stuck a sheet on our cupboard with three headings: DON'T KNOW, CAN FIND OUT CHEAPLY, DECIDE BY. Under the first: "Will I do fieldwork or only data entry? Is there housing near the lab?" Under the second: "Message last year's intern. Ask the NGO for a sample week." Under the third: "Sunday, 8 pm." Below that: "Default: Goa, unless it's only data entry." By Thursday the intern had replied: mostly boat surveys. On Sunday at 7:50 she accepted Goa. I can't say whether she was nervous inside. She just wrote "assumption: fieldwork" beside her choice and went down to dinner.

qa.q: What were the three headings on Preeti's sheet?
qa.a: DON'T KNOW, CAN FIND OUT CHEAPLY and DECIDE BY.

qa.q: How did Preeti seem to feel while deciding, as far as Gopika could tell?
qa.a: She seemed calm and settled, though Gopika admits not knowing whether she was nervous inside.

qa.q: Why was writing "assumption: fieldwork" a smart step?
qa.a: If the lab later turns out to be mostly data entry, Preeti knows exactly which belief was wrong and can rethink quickly instead of starting over.

qa.q: How does Gopika see Preeti's way of choosing?
qa.a: Gopika watches it closely and seems impressed by how orderly it is, especially compared with pacing and worrying.

grounding: Illustrates listing the unknowns, finding out what can be learned cheaply, setting a decision date and a default, and recording the assumption.

passage: On Thursday night at a hawker centre in Singapore, Xin had until noon on Friday to answer two job offers. The logistics company had a training programme and a manager she had liked. The five-person start-up building bus-route software had the more exciting work, but nobody could tell her whether it would survive past the year. "What if I choose the safe one and the start-up turns out to be the big chance?" she said, pushing noodles around. Rafael handed her a napkin. She wrote: I want someone to learn from this year. I don't want to job-hunt again in twelve months. I'd regret boredom less than chaos. She chose the logistics firm and sent the email at 11:40 the next morning, stomach in knots. Eight months later the start-up won a big city contract. Rafael winced at the news. Xin unfolded the napkin. "The reasons were good," she said. "With what I knew, I'd make the same call."

qa.q: What did the start-up build?
qa.a: Bus-route software.

qa.q: How did Xin feel as she sent the email on Friday?
qa.a: She was anxious, with her stomach in knots, afraid that the safe choice might turn out to be the wrong one.

qa.q: What helped Xin judge her decision fairly months later?
qa.a: The napkin kept her reasons, so she could judge the choice by what she knew then, not by the start-up's later luck.

qa.q: Why might Rafael react differently from Xin to the news?
qa.a: Rafael winces, perhaps worried she will feel regret, while Xin looks at the written reasons and stays steady.

grounding: Shows a young professional choosing between two offers with key facts missing, feeling the weight of being wrong, and judging the choice by its reasoning.

passage:
[Family group]
Mummy: Francis, ship job means eight months at sea. What if something happens? 😟
Uncle Joe: Hotel job is steady. Ships come and go. My friend's son came back with nothing.
Aunty Rita: Nonsense, go! Stay in Goa forever and you'll never see the world.
Mummy: Rita, don't encourage him.
Francis: Thank you all, really. I'm listening to every point. I'll decide by Sunday and tell you why.
[Private chat]
Binita: very diplomatic message 😅 you ok?
Francis: honestly my head is spinning. they're all so sure and all saying opposite things
Binita: they're sure about their own fears, not about your life
Francis: mummy's fear is the sea. uncle's is money. aunty's is being stuck
Francis: none of those is exactly mine
Binita: so what's yours?
Francis: missing too many years of home. I'll ask the cruise line about a shorter first contract
Binita: see, that's your own question 👍

qa.q: How long did Mummy say the ship job would keep Francis at sea?
qa.a: Eight months.

qa.q: How is Francis feeling after the family group messages?
qa.a: He is overwhelmed and confused, with his head spinning, because everyone is so sure and says opposite things.

qa.q: What did Francis do well in his reply to the family?
qa.a: He thanked everyone and said he was listening, but kept the decision his own by promising to decide by Sunday and explain why.

qa.q: How does Mummy see the ship job?
qa.a: Mummy sees it through fear for his safety at sea, which is why she worries about what might happen and tells Rita not to encourage him.

grounding: Shows a young man whose relatives each give confident, conflicting career advice from their own fears, and who listens respectfully without handing over the choice.

passage: The rain had turned to hail by the time Reena reached the animal shelter on the Shimla hill road, and the staff were closing early because of a landslide warning. She had twenty minutes. She needed a leash for walking the shelter dogs on weekends; there were two, red and blue. She took the blue without a second look. If she hated it, she could swap it next week. Then the manager asked whether she wanted to adopt Moti, the old brown dog who always leaned on her knees. Reena's chest went warm and tight at once. This couldn't be undone next week. Her landlord hadn't agreed to pets, and her school posting might move her in a year. Under the tin awning she phoned Rukmini, who had kept three rescue dogs. "Ask your landlord first," Rukmini said. "Moti will still be here on Saturday." Reena told the manager she'd come back Saturday with an answer.

qa.q: Which leash did Reena choose?
qa.a: The blue one.

qa.q: What did Reena feel when the manager asked about adopting Moti?
qa.a: She felt warm affection and a tight worry at once, torn between loving Moti and knowing the choice couldn't be undone.

qa.q: Why did Reena treat the two choices so differently?
qa.a: The leash could be swapped next week, so she chose fast; adopting Moti was hard to undo, so she slowed down and asked someone with experience.

qa.q: How might Rukmini see Reena's phone call?
qa.a: Rukmini, who kept three rescue dogs, likely respects that Reena paused, and reassures her calmly that waiting until Saturday costs little.

grounding: Illustrates acting quickly on a choice that is cheap to undo and slowing down to seek advice on one that is not, under time pressure.

subtype: Child frozen or crying at an accident [Actor]
passage:
Monday: At the park, a big boy fell off the slide and his knee bled. Urmila stood very still. Then she cried, loudly. Anand bhaiya, the park guard, came running to help the boy.
Wednesday: At home Urmila told Nani, "I was scared. My feet stopped." Nani hugged her. "That's okay. Next time, step away and find a grown-up, like Anand bhaiya." They practised: step back, run, tell.
Saturday: Urmila's baby cousin bumped his head on the table and screamed. Urmila stepped back, ran to the kitchen and tugged Nani's sari. "Nani, come! Baby fell!" Nani came quickly.

qa.q: Who came running to help the boy at the park?
qa.a: Anand bhaiya, the park guard.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel on Monday at the park?
qa.a: Urmila was scared; she said her feet stopped, and then she cried.

qa.q: What did Nani teach Urmila to do next time?
qa.a: Step back, run and tell a grown-up.

qa.q: How might Nani feel when Urmila tugs her sari on Saturday?
qa.a: Nani is probably worried about the baby but also proud and relieved that Urmila remembered the practice.

grounding: Shows a young child who freezes and cries at an accident, which is normal, and then learns to move away and tell a grown-up.

subtype: Learning emergency numbers and who to tell [Actor]
passage:
Sunday
Today I was so scared my hands shook. Dadi slipped in the bathroom and couldn't get up. She said, "Eshaan, don't pull me, call someone." My head went empty. Then I remembered the card on the fridge that Mama makes us practise every Sunday: 1. Tell a grown-up close by. 2. Call Papa. 3. If it's serious, 112. I ran next door and banged on Baljeet uncle's door. He came with his phone, called 112 and told them our address, Flat 3, Gulmohar Colony. I called Papa like we practised. The ambulance people were kind. Dadi is okay now, just a sore wrist. Baljeet uncle said I did everything right. I think the practising did it, not me being brave.

qa.q: What was the third step on the card on the fridge?
qa.a: If it's serious, 112.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel when Dadi slipped?
qa.a: Eshaan was so scared that the hands shook and the mind went empty.

qa.q: What helped Eshaan act even though fear made thinking hard?
qa.a: The card practised every Sunday: the steps came back in order, so Eshaan fetched Baljeet uncle and called Papa.

qa.q: How might Dadi feel about what Eshaan did?
qa.a: Dadi was probably relieved and proud that Eshaan didn't pull her and quickly got a grown-up.

grounding: Shows a child who has practised emergency steps, numbers and which trusted adult to call, and uses them when fear empties the mind.

passage: At the Thursday market in a village outside Dharwad, a tractor trolley reversing too fast knocked over the potato stall, and its owner went down under the planks. In seconds twenty people stood in a ring. Sudha, sixteen, clutching her mother's shopping bag, stared at the man's leg twisted under the wood. Someone must have called by now, she thought. Everyone had phones out. Nobody was dialling; they were filming or muttering. Then Samir, the schoolteacher who ran the seed shop, pushed through and pointed straight at her. "You, green dupatta. Call 108. Say Thursday market, near the water tank." Sudha's fingers shook, but she dialled. Samir pointed at two men: "You two, lift only the planks, slowly. Nobody move him." The operator asked questions and Sudha answered each one, reading landmarks off the signboard. She stayed on the line until the siren came up the dusty road.

qa.q: How many people stood in a ring around the fallen stall?
qa.a: Twenty people.

qa.q: What was Sudha feeling and assuming before Samir pointed at her?
qa.a: She was shocked and frozen, assuming someone must already have called because everyone had phones out.

qa.q: Why did Samir's pointing work when the crowd did nothing?
qa.a: Naming one person with one clear task made the responsibility hers, so it no longer felt shared by everyone and done by no one.

qa.q: What is it like for the stall owner while twenty people only film?
qa.a: He is hurt and trapped under the planks while people watch, so he is likely frightened and alone until someone finally calls and help comes.

grounding: Shows a teenager in a crowd at an accident assuming someone else has called, until being named as the one to call breaks the spell.

subtype: Basic first aid course and calm hands [Actor]
passage:
Saturday: At the college first-aid workshop, the instructor made Ritu repeat it until it bored her: "Danger. Call. Press. And don't do anything you weren't taught."
Two weeks later, Thursday: A glass slipped from Karthik's hand in the hostel kitchen and a long shard sliced his palm. Blood dripped fast onto the floor, and he swore at himself, furious. Ritu's stomach flipped, but the words came in order. She kicked the broken pieces away from their feet. "Mehul, call the warden and ask for the doctor, now." She folded a clean tea towel, pressed it hard on the cut and held his hand up. A tiny sliver glinted near the edge. She wanted to pick it out. She didn't.
Friday: Karthik came back with stitches and a bandage. "The doctor took out a piece of glass," he said. "Said the pressure helped." Ritu nodded. "I nearly tried to take it out myself."

qa.q: What did Ritu press on Karthik's cut?
qa.a: A folded clean tea towel.

qa.q: How was Ritu feeling when she saw the blood?
qa.a: Her stomach flipped with fear, but she stayed calm enough for the practised words to come in order.

qa.q: Which of Ritu's choices shows she knew her limits?
qa.a: She wanted to pick out the glass sliver but didn't, leaving it for the doctor and sticking to pressure, which she had been taught.

qa.q: How might Karthik see the moment afterwards?
qa.a: Karthik was angry at himself during it, and afterwards is probably grateful, since the doctor said the pressure helped.

grounding: Shows a trained young adult who clears danger, sends for help, applies pressure as taught and holds back from doing more than she was trained for.

passage:
Warden's note, Tuesday night.
At about 9:15 a delivery rider skidded on the wet road outside our gate and lay on his side, groaning. His name, we later learned, was Jatin. Binita, a second-year resident with no first-aid training, was first out of the gate. I could see she was shaking. She still did things in order. She asked our watchman to stand in the road with his torch and slow the cars. She called 112 and put the phone on speaker. When Jatin tried to sit up and pull off his helmet, she knelt beside him and said, "Please stay still, help is coming," because the operator had told her not to move him. She kept talking to him, asked his name, told the operator he was awake and breathing. She stayed until the ambulance took him. Afterwards I sat with her over tea; she cried a little. Tomorrow I'll ask the college about a first-aid session for residents.

qa.q: Who did Binita ask to slow the cars?
qa.a: The watchman, standing in the road with his torch.

qa.q: How was Binita feeling as she helped, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She was frightened, shaking and crying a little afterwards, yet focused enough to do each step in order.

qa.q: Which of Binita's steps protected Jatin most, and why?
qa.a: Keeping him still instead of letting him sit up or take off the helmet, as the operator said, because moving a badly hurt person can make things worse.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Jatin lying on the wet road?
qa.a: He was likely scared and confused, and a calm voice asking his name and saying help was coming would have made him feel less alone.

grounding: Shows an untrained, scared person keeping the scene safe, calling emergency services, staying with the injured rider and following the operator's advice not to move him.
